analysis.headline: Introduced June 16, 2026 by Sen. Schumer and six Democratic colleagues, referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has taken place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would quadruple the federal excise tax on corporate stock buybacks — when a company buys back its own shares — from 1% to 4% of the value repurchased [S2]. It would also close an offset companies can currently use: today, the tax is reduced by the value of new stock a company issues during the year, but the bill would stop that reduction for stock given to executives or to anyone paid more than $1 million a year [S2]. In plain terms, a company could no longer offset the cost of the buyback tax by handing out shares to its highest-paid people.
analysis.who_benefits: The benefit is diffuse. The federal Treasury would collect more excise-tax revenue from companies that repurchase stock [S2], and every taxpayer benefits indirectly from added revenue. To the extent the higher tax discourages buybacks, the gains are spread broadly across the market rather than delivered to any specific group of households.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1 percent to 4 percent, making large buybacks meaningfully more expensive for companies that choose them.

Ends an offset that currently reduces the tax by the value of newly issued stock: stock issued to covered executives or to any employee or service provider earning over $1 million a year would no longer count against the tax, so companies could not dilute their way out of the levy while rewarding top earners.
An excise tax on buybacks is a source of federal revenue that falls on corporations conducting repurchases rather than on wages or ordinary consumer transactions.

The new rate and the new exception apply to repurchases and stock issuances after enactment, with a proration rule so companies cannot game the transition by front-loading repurchases within the enactment-year taxable year.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase their own stock would pay the 4% excise tax — four times the current 1% — on every buyback after enactment [S2]. The most concentrated new cost falls on highly paid insiders: executives and anyone earning over $1 million a year would lose the stock-issuance offset that today reduces a company's buyback tax bill, so compensation paid in stock would no longer lower the company's tax [S2].

drawbacks.text: The tax is collected from the corporation, but the cost of a buyback tax can ultimately be borne by shareholders — including mutual funds, pension funds, and 401(k) savers who hold the stock — rather than only by executives.

A 4% levy is still small relative to the total value of a buyback, so it may raise modest revenue and change little corporate behavior; a company determined to repurchase shares pays the tax and proceeds.
Taxing buybacks but not dividends skews corporate choices between the two ways of returning cash to shareholders, and companies may simply shift to dividends or other uses of cash to avoid the levy.

The bill has no Republican support in the record — all seven cosponsors are Democrats — and tax increases face steep odds in the Senate Finance Committee, where the bill sits without a scheduled hearing or markup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, narrowly designed bill, not a sweeping one. Its real substance is the executive-compensation loophole: without the new exception, a company could issue a wave of shares to top earners and largely erase the buyback tax [S2]. The revenue and the behavioral nudge from raising the rate to 4% are real but small, and the honest objections are serious: the cost can flow to ordinary shareholders through fund holdings, and companies can dodge the effect by switching to dividends. On balance, the bill imposes a genuine, targeted cost on buyback-heavy corporations and their highly paid executives while offering ordinary people only indirect, diffuse gains — a reasonable policy lever, but not one that delivers a tangible benefit to most households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and has seen no further action; no vote has occurred.

narrative.text: On June 16, 2026, Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Stock Buyback Accountability Act of 2026, joined by Sens. Wyden, Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
The bill has seven cosponsors, all Democrats.
The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or further referral has been recorded.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically still alive but has taken no step toward a vote.

key_actors.name: Charles E. Schumer
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 16, 2026 and assembled six Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors; the bill was then referred to Finance.

key_actors.name: Ron Wyden
key_actors.role: Chair, Senate Finance Committee (D-OR); original cosponsor
key_actors.what_they_did: Cosponsored and helped introduce the bill, which was referred to the Finance Committee he chairs; the record shows no markup or hearing scheduled.

key_actors.name: Senate Finance Committee
key_actors.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 16, 2026; per the action history, it has taken no recorded action on the bill since.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces a steep path. It sits in the Senate Finance Committee with roughly six and a half months left in the Congress, no scheduled hearing or markup, no Republican cosponsors, and no companion action in the House in the record. Tax bills at this stage overwhelmingly die when the Congress ends unless they are folded into a larger legislative package; absent that, expect S. 4796 to expire without a vote when the 119th Congress adjourns on January 3, 2027.
